record.paper_title: Cyber-Physical Attacks on UAS Networks–Challenges and Open Research Problems
record.context_brief: Secure UAV ADS-B and TCAS adaptation
record.original_question: How can UAV air-traffic-control and collision-avoidance systems based on ADS-B- or TCAS-like protocols be redesigned or secured so that unauthenticated broadcasts, false traffic-data injection, and intentionally orchestrated TCAS-induced collision scenarios do not create unsafe advisories in mission-critical UAS operations?

evidence.quote: Recent literature contain several proposals on TCAS and ATC solutions for UAVs, many of which are based on adaptation of ADS-B and commercial TCAS protocols. From a security point of view, this approach suffers from several critical vulnerabilities, rendering it unfeasible for mission-critical UAS applications. Firstly, ADS-B is an insecure protocol by design [1]. Lack of authentication and the unencrypted broadcast nature of this protocol make room for relatively simple attacks, ranging from eavesdropping to manipulation of air traffic data by jamming or injection of false data.

Also, TCAS is shown to be susceptible to a flaw known as “TCAS-Induced Collisions” [9]. Common implementations of TCAS are not equipped with prediction capabilities to foresee the longer-term effect of an advisory that they produce. In dense traffic conditions, certain scenarios may cause the TCAS to generate advisories that lead to a state where avoidance of collision is not possible. Hence, an adversary capable of manipulating the traffic data can intentionally orchestrate conditions leading to TCAS-induced collisions.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider an unmanned aerial system (UAS) operating in shared airspace and equipped with an air-traffic-control (ATC) and collision-avoidance system modeled on the Automatic Dependent Surveillance–Broadcast (ADS-B) protocol and the Traffic Alert and Collision Avoidance System (TCAS). In the standard ADS-B model, every aircraft periodically broadcasts, in cleartext and without cryptographic authentication, a state vector consisting of its identifier, position, velocity, and altitude; any receiver within radio range accepts these messages as authentic. In the standard TCAS model, each aircraft uses received state vectors of nearby traffic to issue local resolution advisories (climb/descend/turn) computed from short-horizon pairwise extrapolation, without global multi-aircraft prediction.

Consider an adversary with the following capabilities:
(a) eavesdropping on all ADS-B broadcasts in a region;
(b) jamming legitimate ADS-B transmissions;
(c) injecting forged ADS-B messages with arbitrary state vectors attributed to arbitrary identifiers (ghost aircraft) at chosen times;
(d) choosing the spatial-temporal pattern of injected traffic so as to drive the TCAS logic of one or more victim UAVs into a configuration in which any sequence of advisories produced by the standard TCAS rules leads, within the short prediction horizon, to a state from which collision is unavoidable (a "TCAS-induced collision" scenario).

Design a redesigned ATC/collision-avoidance protocol suite for UASs, replacing or augmenting ADS-B and TCAS, satisfying all of the following requirements simultaneously:

1. Message authenticity and integrity: every accepted state-vector message can be cryptographically attributed to a legitimate, authorized airspace participant, so that injected ghost-aircraft messages are rejected with overwhelming probability under a computationally bounded adversary.
2. Confidentiality where required: sensitive mission data carried alongside surveillance broadcasts is not readable by passive eavesdroppers, while remaining verifiable by authorized ATC entities.
3. Jamming resilience: the protocol degrades gracefully under partial denial-of-service of the broadcast channel, preserving safe-separation guarantees with quantifiable probability.
4. Long-horizon collision-avoidance soundness: the advisory-generation algorithm, taking as input the set of authenticated state vectors, never issues an advisory sequence that drives the local UAV into a state from which collision is unavoidable, provided the authenticated traffic picture is consistent with feasible aircraft dynamics.
5. Backward compatibility: the protocol can interoperate with legacy ADS-B/TCAS-equipped manned aircraft in mixed airspace without compromising properties (1)–(4) for the UAS participants.

Provide such a protocol, together with a precise adversary model and proofs (or rigorous arguments) that properties (1)–(5) hold; or prove that no protocol satisfying all five properties simultaneously can exist under stated assumptions.
artifact.status_search_result: Securing ADS-B and designing UAS-suitable collision-avoidance schemes that simultaneously address authentication, jamming resilience, and TCAS-induced-collision avoidance remain active research topics. Multiple partial proposals (e.g., ADS-B authentication via lightweight signatures, secure broadcast schemes, ACAS Xu for UAS) exist, but no widely accepted solution meets all the stated requirements together; the problem is generally treated as open in the literature on UAS cyber-physical security.

status_evidence.title: Cyber-Physical Attacks on UAS Networks—Challenges and Open Research Problems
status_evidence.snippet: Identifies ADS-B insecurity and TCAS-induced collisions as open challenges for mission-critical UAS.
status_evidence.claim: The problem is posed as an open research challenge.
